newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions, firms urge cut to labour costs.
newsitem.headline: German unions, firms urge cut to labour costs.

text.p: Germany's trade union and employer federations are uniting to call for the country's high non-wage labour costs to be cut in a bid to ease existing high jobless levels, it was reported on Thursday.

For every one mark earned in salary, German employers and employees are currently estimated to have to pay as much as 80 pfennigs between them into a variety of work insurance and other social schemes.

Both sides want the government to strip non-work-related payments out of existing employee and employer contributions in a move they say would reduce total labour costs -- seen as among the highest in the world -- by a huge 60 billion marks.

"German wages are not too high on an international scale. What is too high, however, are the additional non-wage costs," Dieter Hundt, president of the German employers federation BDA, was widely quoted in German newspapers as saying.
Both Hundt and Dieter Schulte, head of the German Federation of Trade Unions (DGB), want payments to schemes that are not directly related to employment to be taken out of contributions.
"On one point I share the view of the employers -- too great a cost burden is placed on work in Germany. Employment and labour costs are linked," Schulte said.

The savings from such a move would vastly outweigh the estimated benefit of a highly controversial law brought in last October to cut sick pay entitlements but which, following mass worker protests, many employers have not dared to implement.

By reducing employers' labour costs, it is argued, companies would be more inclined to invest in new job positions, thus easing unemployment figures that have risen to a post-unification high of four million.

Hundt called on the Bonn government to keep to an earlier promise that social contributions should fall below 40 percent of an employee's gross salary. He estimated that in 1997 such costs would if any thing rise slightly to 42 percent.

Hans Peter Stihl, president of the German Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), noted that without a reduction in labour costs, and particularly non-wage costs, the 2.5 percent economic growth widely forecast for Germany in 1997 would not lead to more jobs.
"Only a growth rate of three percent or more will lead to an appreciable reduction in unemployment," Stihl said in a statement.

The apparent consensus on non-wage costs comes after a number of wage agreements between unions and employers in which unions have settled on inflation-related 1997 pay rises in return for maintenance of sick pay at full salary.
Economists have said the 1997 wage accords reached in industries such as the engineering and chemical sectors will result in an almost insignificant increase in overall wage costs this year.
While unions and employers agree that social costs should fall, there is sharp disagreement on what measures need to be taken to recoup the resulting shortfall in contributions to social investment.
Unions believe that a value-added tax could be introduced to counter-balance the reduction, while employers argue that such a measure is not necessary and social spending needs to fall.
